articles.title: Google Antigravity 2.0: Gemini CLI Dies June 18, Full Agentic Dev Platform Takes Over
articles.tldr: At Google I/O 2026, Google launched Antigravity 2.0 — upgrading its agentic coding tool into a full developer platform with a redesigned desktop app, a new CLI built in Go, and an SDK for custom agent workflows. Gemini CLI consumer access ends June 18, 2026, forcing migration to the new platform.
articles.why_it_matters: This is Google's biggest bet on agentic development. Antigravity 2.0 shares the same agent harness across desktop, CLI, and SDK — meaning improvements to core agents propagate everywhere automatically. Developers can now run parallel agents, design custom subagent workflows, and schedule background tasks. The June 18 Gemini CLI sunset is a hard deadline: if your team uses Gemini CLI, migration planning starts now.

articles.title: Kimi K2.6: The 1-Trillion-Parameter Open-Weight Model Leading Agentic Coding
articles.tldr: Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6 is a 1-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters, released under a Modified MIT License. It leads open-weight benchmarks for agentic coding with reliable multi-language support (Rust, Go, Python) and long-horizon execution — 4,000+ tool calls over 12 hours in a single session.
articles.why_it_matters: Kimi K2.6 is the model that makes self-hosted agentic coding viable at frontier quality. With 1T total / 32B active parameters, 262K context window, and INT4 quantization out of the box, teams can run a frontier-class coding agent on their own infrastructure. The 12-hour continuous execution capability means it can handle the kind of long-running refactoring and migration tasks that previously required cloud-only models.

articles.title: OpenAI Codex + GPT-5.5 Go GA on AWS Bedrock: Enterprise Multi-Cloud Coding Agents
articles.tldr: OpenAI's Codex coding agent, powered by GPT-5.5, is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock as of June 1, 2026. Over 4 million developers use Codex weekly, and they can now run it through AWS with IAM authentication, VPC isolation, encryption, and pricing that counts toward existing AWS commitments.
articles.why_it_matters: This is the first time a frontier coding agent is available as a first-class AWS service. Enterprise teams that couldn't adopt Codex due to security or procurement constraints now get it through their existing AWS stack — same IAM, same VPC, same billing. GPT-5.5 scores 82.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 58.6% on SWE-Bench Pro. The multi-cloud pattern (Codex on AWS, not just OpenAI's API) signals that coding agents are becoming infrastructure, not features.

articles.title: MCP Goes Stateless: The Protocol Update That Makes Agent Deployment Actually Simple
articles.tldr: The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) is releasing a major MCP update that makes the protocol stateless at the transport layer. No more session IDs, sticky sessions, or shared session stores — each request is self-contained with version, client info, and capabilities traveling with the payload. Release candidate is available now; final spec ships July 28, 2026.
articles.why_it_matters: Sticky sessions were the hidden tax on every MCP deployment. Load balancers needed MCP-aware routing, horizontal scaling required shared session stores, and gateway failures broke agent sessions. Stateless MCP eliminates all of this — standard HTTP load balancers, CDN caching, and serverless functions just work. Application-level state becomes explicit (server returns a handle, model passes it back) instead of hidden in transport metadata. This is MCP growing from a clever demo protocol into production infrastructure.

articles.title: NVIDIA OpenShell: Kernel-Level Agent Sandboxing with Declarative YAML Policies
articles.tldr: NVIDIA's OpenShell is an open-source, policy-driven sandbox runtime for autonomous AI agents. It enforces security at the kernel level via Landlock LSM and Seccomp BPF — agents run inside individual sandboxes with declarative YAML policies controlling filesystem, network, process execution, and inference calls. Policies hot-reload without restarts and every allow/deny decision gets a full audit trail.
articles.why_it_matters: Microsoft's MXC (covered yesterday) sandboxes agents at the OS level on Windows. NVIDIA's OpenShell does the same for Linux — and it's open source. The combination means agent sandboxing is becoming a platform primitive across both operating systems. For teams running agents in production on Linux (which is most of them), OpenShell is the missing security layer: kernel-enforced policies that agents literally cannot bypass, with hot-reload so you can tighten policies on running agents without downtime.

articles.title: Claude Agent SDK: Build Production Agents with the Same Engine That Powers Claude Code
articles.tldr: Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK gives developers the same agent loop, tools, and context management infrastructure that powers Claude Code — available in Python and TypeScript with first-class MCP support. Custom tools run as in-process MCP servers, eliminating separate processes. Starting June 15, 2026, Agent SDK usage gets its own billing credit separate from interactive usage.
articles.why_it_matters: The Agent SDK is Anthropic's play to make Claude Code's architecture the default for custom agent development. In-process MCP servers mean you can build tool-using agents without the overhead of running separate MCP server processes — tools are just Python/TypeScript functions with MCP semantics. The June 15 billing split signals that Anthropic sees programmatic agent usage as a distinct product category from chat, and wants to price it separately to encourage adoption.

articles.title: AI-Powered CI Hits 76% Adoption: Platform Engineering Becomes the Default Operating Model
articles.tldr: Industry data shows 76% of DevOps teams now use AI-powered CI to reduce manual work and speed delivery. Platform Engineering has emerged as the dominant approach — building internal developer platforms as products with self-service layers that abstract infrastructure complexity. Framework adoption nearly doubled from 9% to 18% year-over-year.
articles.why_it_matters: The shift from 'DevOps team runs CI' to 'platform team ships a self-service product' is now the majority pattern, not an aspiration. AI-powered CI isn't just faster pipelines — it's automated test selection, intelligent flaky test quarantine, and PR risk scoring. Teams still running traditional Jenkins/GitLab CI without AI augmentation are falling behind on both speed and developer experience. The 76% number means this is no longer early adoption; it's table stakes.

articles.title: OpenClaw Ships Skill Security: SkillSpector, Pre-Publish Verification, and a Public Safety Dataset
articles.tldr: OpenClaw's 2026.6.1-alpha.3 release focuses on agent governance: ClawHub skills now require pre-publish verification, NVIDIA Skill Cards provide standardized metadata, and SkillSpector performs automated risk analysis before skills go live. OpenClaw also published a public dataset of scan outcomes on Hugging Face to help the broader community improve agent skill safety.
articles.why_it_matters: As agent ecosystems grow, skill/plugin marketplaces become the new npm — and yesterday's codexui-android supply chain attack proves the risk is real. OpenClaw's approach — verification before publish, automated risk scoring, and a public safety dataset — is the kind of proactive governance that prevents agent skill stores from becoming attack vectors. The public dataset on HuggingFace means other platforms can build on this work instead of reinventing trust signals from scratch.

articles.title: O'Reilly Radar June 2026: The Trends That Should Actually Change What You Build
articles.tldr: O'Reilly's June 2026 Radar highlights the convergence of agentic AI with production infrastructure: agent sandboxing becoming an OS primitive, MCP evolving into a stateless standard, and the gap widening between organizations that treat AI as infrastructure versus those still running pilots. The report flags agent skill marketplaces as the next supply chain attack surface.
articles.why_it_matters: O'Reilly's Radar is the canary for what enterprise engineering leadership reads. When they flag agent sandboxing and MCP statelessness in the same issue, it means these aren't niche concerns anymore — they're entering the enterprise planning cycle. The supply chain warning aligns with this week's codexui-android attack. If you're pitching agent infrastructure investments internally, this report is the executive summary your VP of Engineering needs to see.
